children.funFact: The purple-striped jelly (Pelagia noctiluca) is one of the few jellyfish that can produce bioluminescence, creating beautiful blue-green flashes of light when disturbed in dark water.

children.name: Ulmaridae
Aurelia
children.description: Moon jellies are translucent, bell-shaped jellyfish that drift through coastal waters with a graceful, pulsing motion. They are among the most recognizable jellyfish, with their characteristic saucer-like bodies and delicate, trailing tentacles that help them capture small prey like plankton and tiny fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Moon jellies can be identified by their four distinctive horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs visible through their transparent bell, along with their relatively mild sting compared to other jellyfish species.
children.funFact: Moon jellies are about 95% water and have no brain, blood, or heart, yet they've been drifting through Earth's oceans for over 500 million years!

children.description: Ulmarid jellies are a family of true jellyfish that includes some of the most recognizable and common jellies found in New England waters. These graceful creatures are characterized by their bell-shaped, translucent bodies and relatively mild stings that are generally harmless to humans. They are excellent swimmers that pulse through the water column feeding on small plankton and fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ulmarid jellies can be distinguished from other jellyfish families by their four distinct horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs (gonads) that are clearly visible through their transparent bell. They also typically have short, numerous tentacles around the bell margin rather than long trailing tentacles.
children.funFact: Moon jellies, the most famous members of this family, have been used in space research - they were sent to space in 1991 to study how microgravity affects their development, since their simple nervous system is similar to early human neural development.

children.name: Phacellophoridae
Phacellophora
children.description: Phacellophora is a genus of large jellyfish known for their distinctive yellow-orange coloration and impressive size. These jellies are among the largest found in New England waters and are characterized by their bell-shaped body and long, trailing tentacles that can extend many feet below the bell.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Phacellophora apart from other jellyfish is their bright egg-yolk yellow color and their exceptionally long tentacles, which can reach lengths of up to 20 feet or more.
children.funFact: The Egg-yolk Jelly can have a bell diameter of up to 2 feet across, making it one of the largest jellyfish species you might encounter while exploring New England's coastal waters.

children.description: Egg-yolk jellies are large, spectacular jellyfish named for their distinctive golden-yellow coloration that resembles a fried egg floating in the water. These jellies have a flattened, saucer-like bell with numerous long, trailing tentacles that can extend many feet below their body. They are graceful swimmers found in cooler ocean waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other jellyfish, egg-yolk jellies have a distinctly flattened bell shape rather than a dome, and their bright yellow-orange coloration makes them unmistakable in the water.
children.funFact: The fried egg jellyfish can have tentacles that stretch up to 20 feet long, making them appear much larger than their bell size would suggest!

children.description: Flag-mouth Jellies are true jellyfish with four distinct oral arms that hang down from their bell like ribbons or flags. These graceful swimmers have a classic jellyfish shape with a dome-like bell and long, flowing tentacles around the edges, plus those characteristic mouth arms used for capturing and eating prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jellyfish orders, Flag-mouth Jellies have exactly four prominent oral arms extending from their mouth, which gives them their distinctive flaglike appearance when swimming.
children.funFact: The largest jellyfish in the world belongs to this group - the Lion's Mane Jellyfish can have a bell diameter larger than a blue whale and tentacles longer than a football field!

children.name: Rhizostomeae
Stomolophidae
Stomolophus
children.description: Cannonball Jellies are robust, dome-shaped jellyfish with thick, sturdy bells that resemble cannonballs when viewed from above. These jellies are characterized by their distinctive feeding appendages called oral arms that hang beneath their bell, giving them a frilly appearance. They are strong swimmers that can actively propel themselves through the water rather than simply drifting with currents.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other jellyfish, Cannonball Jellies lack long trailing tentacles and instead have short, thick oral arms with feeding grooves. Their bells are notably firm and muscular compared to the more gelatinous consistency of most other jellyfish.
children.funFact: Cannonball Jellies are considered a delicacy in some Asian cuisines and are commercially harvested, with their firm texture making them one of the few jellyfish species regularly eaten by humans.

children.description: Cannonball Jellies are robust, dome-shaped jellyfish with thick, sturdy bells that lack the long, trailing tentacles found in many other jellyfish. Instead, they have short, clustered oral arms around their mouth that help them capture small prey like plankton and fish eggs. These jellies are strong swimmers and are often found in coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most jellyfish, Cannonball Jellies have very short or no marginal tentacles hanging from their bell, and their thick, muscular bell gives them a distinctive cannonball-like appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating size, Cannonball Jellies have a relatively mild sting that's generally harmless to humans, making them one of the safer jellyfish to encounter while swimming.

children.description: Root-mouth jellies are fascinating jellyfish that have evolved a unique feeding system where their mouth has been replaced by many small openings along branching, root-like arms. These jellyfish capture tiny plankton and other small prey using these specialized feeding arms that hang down from their bell like underwater roots. They are among the more advanced jellyfish, having developed this complex feeding structure over millions of years of evolution.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical jellyfish with a single central mouth, root-mouth jellies have completely lost their central mouth opening and instead feed through numerous tiny pores scattered along their thick, branching oral arms.
children.funFact: The branching feeding arms of root-mouth jellies contain millions of tiny mouths that work together like a living filtration system, allowing them to process enormous volumes of water to extract microscopic food particles.

children.name: Stauromedusae
Lucernariidae
Lucernaria
children.description: Lucernaria is a genus of unique marine animals known as stalked jellyfish that look more like sea anemones than typical jellyfish. These fascinating creatures attach themselves to seaweed, rocks, or other surfaces in shallow coastal waters using a muscular stalk. Unlike free-swimming jellyfish, they remain anchored in one spot and capture small prey with their ring of tentacles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lucernaria species are distinguished by their goblet or trumpet-shaped body mounted on a flexible stalk, with clusters of tentacles arranged around the rim of their bell-like top.
children.funFact: Despite being called jellyfish, Lucernaria can actually crawl along surfaces by bending their stalk and using their tentacles like tiny legs to move to new locations.

children.description: Lucernariidae is a family of unusual marine animals called stalked jellies that look more like sea anemones than typical jellyfish. These fascinating creatures attach themselves to seaweed, rocks, or other surfaces in shallow coastal waters using a stalk-like base, rather than swimming freely like most jellyfish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike free-swimming jellyfish, members of this family are sessile (attached to surfaces) and have a distinctive trumpet or goblet shape with eight clusters of tentacles around the rim.
children.funFact: Stalked jellies can actually crawl along surfaces by detaching their base and using a somersaulting motion to relocate to a better spot!

children.description: Stauromedusae are unique jellyfish that have given up the free-swimming lifestyle to become attached to surfaces like rocks and seaweed. Unlike typical jellyfish that drift through the water, these creatures look more like small stalked flowers or trumpets anchored to the seafloor. They are commonly called stalked jellies or upside-down jellies because of their distinctive shape and lifestyle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jellyfish, stauromedusae are sessile (attached to surfaces) and have a trumpet-shaped body with adhesive anchors at the base. They lack the typical bell-shaped, free-swimming form of most jellyfish and instead have eight clusters of short tentacles arranged around their upward-facing mouth.
children.funFact: These stalked jellies can actually walk along the seafloor by detaching from one spot and using a somersaulting motion to relocate to a better feeding position.
